title: Subject-verb agreement
keyIdea: The subject is who or what does the action, and the verb is the action. They must agree, or match. When the subject is one person or thing, like he, she, it or the dog, add s to the verb: the dog runs. When the subject is more than one, like they, we or the dogs, the verb has no s: the dogs run. I and you also take no s: I run. Use is with one and are with more than one.

kid: A sentence tells us who does something. The who is the subject. The doing word is the verb. In Mia kicks the ball, Mia is the subject and kicks is the verb.
The verb has to match the subject. One dog runs. Two dogs run. Look: only one word gets the s. With one dog, the s is on runs. With two dogs, the s is on dogs.
He, she and it are one, so the verb gets an s: she sings. They and we are more than one, so no s: they sing. I and you never get the s: I sing.
Is and are work the same way. The cat is sleepy. The cats are sleepy. Tom and Ana are friends, because that is two people.
adult: Subject-verb agreement means the verb's form matches the number and person of its subject. In the present tense, English marks this in only one place: a third-person singular subject (he, she, it, the dog, Mia) takes a verb with the -s or -es suffix. Every other subject (I, you, we, they, the dogs) takes the plain verb. Common Core L.1.1c asks Grade 1 children to use singular and plural nouns with matching verbs in basic sentences (He hops; We hop), and L.3.1f returns to it. In England, Key Stage 1 grammar builds the terms noun, verb, singular and plural, and Year 4 asks for Standard English verb forms such as we were, not we was.

Key words: subject (who or what does the action), verb (the action word), singular (one), plural (more than one), present tense, the suffix -s or -es, pronoun (he, she, it, they, we, I, you), and agree. Be is irregular: I am, he is, they are. Have works the same way: she has, they have. After s, sh, ch or x the verb takes -es: she washes, he fixes.

Common mistakes: putting an s on both the noun and the verb (the dogs runs), because children link s with more than one; adding s after I (I runs); using is after two names joined by and (Tom and Ana is); adding s after irregular plurals such as children or people (the children plays); and writing washs in place of washes. A careful check is to find the subject first, ask whether it is one or more, then fix the verb.

In the lab your child taps the subject in three sentences, drags a single s to either the noun or the verb as the picture changes from one frog to three, picks the verb for he, they and I, chooses is or are, and taps the one wrong verb in three sentences to fix it. Every drag has a big button twin.

familyTip: Play the s swap at dinner. Say 'One cat naps.' Then hold up three fingers and let your child say 'Three cats nap.' Ask them where the s went. Swap in he, they and I as well.

visual.caption: Does the verb need an s? Drag each subject, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: find the subject, swap the s between noun and verb, match verbs to he, they and I, choose is or are, fix wrong verbs.

practice.prompt: Pick the verb that agrees with the subject: The bird ___ in the tree.
practice.hint: Is the subject one bird or more than one? One subject means the verb takes s.
practice.explain: The bird is one, so the verb takes s: the bird sings. Sing would need more birds, and singing needs a helper like is.

practice.prompt: In 'The dog runs', only one word ends in s. In 'The dogs run', only one word ends in s too. You write {n} sentences like these. How many s endings do you write?
practice.hint: Each sentence has exactly one s: on the verb for one dog, or on the noun for many dogs.
practice.explain: Each sentence has one s, so {n} sentences have {n} s endings. The s never goes on both words.

practice.hint: They means more than one. Does the verb need an s?
practice.explain: They play is right: they is plural, so no s. Plays is for one, and they goes with are, not is.

practice.prompt: There are {n} ducks on the pond. In 'The ducks swim', how many ducks does the subject stand for?
practice.hint: The subject is the ducks. Count the ducks on the pond.
practice.explain: The ducks stands for all {n} ducks. Because {n} is more than one, the verb is swim, with no s.

pool.prompt: What is the subject in 'The tall girl jumps high'?
pool.hint: Ask yourself: who is doing the jumping? That whole group of words is the subject.
pool.explain: The tall girl does the jumping, so she is the subject. Jumps is the verb, and high tells how.

pool.prompt: Pick the right verb: The frogs ___ into the pond.
pool.hint: Frogs already has an s. Only one word gets the s.
pool.explain: The frogs is more than one, so the verb has no s: the frogs hop. Hopes is a different word.

pool.prompt: Pick the right verb: I ___ my teeth.
pool.hint: I and you never take the s.
pool.explain: I brush is right. He brushes takes es after sh, but I takes the plain verb.

pool.prompt: Pick the right word: Sam and Leo ___ at the park.
pool.hint: Two names joined by and make more than one.
pool.explain: Sam and Leo are two people, so use are. Is is for one, and am only goes with I.

pool.hint: Children means more than one child, even without an s.
pool.explain: The children plays is wrong: children is plural, so the verb is play. One child plays.

pool.prompt: Pick the right verb: She ___ the window.
pool.hint: She is one person. After x, the verb ending is es.
pool.explain: She fixes is right. After s, sh, ch or x, add es, so fixs is not a word, and fix needs a plural subject.

pool.prompt: The {n} cats nap on the bed. Then all but one walk away. How many cats are left? (Then 'The cats nap' turns into 'The cat naps'.)
pool.hint: Take away all the cats but one. One cat left means the verb changes.
pool.explain: All but one walk away, so 1 cat is left. Now the cat naps, with an s on the verb.

pool.prompt: Which sentence about a pet is correct?
pool.hint: Have works like other verbs: she has, they have.
pool.explain: My dog has a ball is right: one dog takes has. My dogs would need have.

choices: Both words have an s; only one should
pool.hint: Count the words with an s on the end.
pool.explain: More than one dog means the s is on dogs, so the verb is bark: the dogs bark.

pool.prompt: {n} friends each write one sentence about one pet, like 'My cat sleeps.' How many verbs in all end in s?
pool.hint: Each sentence has one pet, so each verb gets an s. Count the sentences.
pool.explain: One pet is singular, so every verb takes s: my cat sleeps. {n} sentences give {n} verbs with s.
